# Debug runs from your coding agent

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

`atira mcp` makes the CLI an MCP server, so Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents can read your runs
and debug them with you: find the failing step in the logs, see the browser's screen at that moment, check what the
agent clicked and typed, then start the next test run. It uses the CLI's sign-in, so there is nothing new to set up.

## Set it up

Install the CLI and sign in once ([CLI guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md)):

```sh
curl -fsSL $API/install.sh | sh
atira login
```

Then add the server to your coding agent:

```sh
claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp     # Claude Code
codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp      # Codex
```

Other clients (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop, ...) take the usual `mcpServers` entry:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "atira": { "command": "atira", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

For Codex you can also write it in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.atira]
command = "atira"
args = ["mcp"]
```

If your editor can't find `atira`, give its full path: `command -v atira` prints it. `ATIRA_TOKEN` works instead of
the stored sign-in, and `atira mcp --help` prints these lines.

## Tools

| Tool | What it does | About |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `challenge_brief` | The challenge: task, websites, rules and limits, run contract, scoring and answer schema | 6k tokens |
| `list_runs` | Your team's recent test and scored runs: status, quality, cost, time and package | 50 tokens a run |
| `get_run` | One run: status and failure, queue place or warm-up while it waits, phases, package, model calls by model with failures and queue waits, points per field, recordings, answer, run page | 1–2k |
| `diagnose_run` | Why a run failed and whether to rerun it as it is: the failure class, the last 20 stdout and stderr lines, model errors, idle stretches over 60 s, browsers whose screen froze | 2–3k |
| `run_logs` | Log lines in time order, by time (`from`, `to`), stream, text (`grep`) and `browser`; `tail` for the last lines; page by page | 30 a line |
| `run_llm_calls` | Every model call, one line each, under a header with time in calls, p50/p95 latency, the most calls at once, failures by status and, for models the organizers host, the queue wait | 35 a call |
| `run_profile` | Where the time went, per 30 s, 1 min or 5 min: inputs and screen activity per browser, model calls, seconds and cost; then the critical path | 1.5–3k |
| `run_screenshot` | A browser's screen at a time with the clicks just before it marked, every browser at once (`browser: "all"`), or a filmstrip (`frames`) | 1.5k an image |
| `run_inputs` | The clicks, scrolls and typing the platform recorded in each browser, with their times | 25 an input |
| `compare_runs` | Two runs side by side: package, quality, time, cost, cost × time, calls and failures per model, phases, points per field and answer fields that changed | 1–2k |
| `wait_for_run` | Wait until a run is running or done, including recording collection and scoring (at most `timeout_s`, default 50 s), then say how it stands | 300 |
| `list_submissions` | Your scored submissions: review status, any organizer note, result and package | 60 a submission |
| `get_submission` | One submission (`sub_...`): review status, any organizer note, its runs | 300–800 |
| `run_package` | The package a run or submission used, as uploaded: SHA-256, label, agent.json and each file's size, never the contents; `out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder | 15 a file |
| `leaderboard` | The board with each entry's cost × time and the Pareto front, your rank and the gap to the next; `compare_run` places one of your runs on it | 500 |
| `models` | The models the organizers host, if any, and how to call them from your computer through `atira models proxy` | 300 |
| `test_run` | Pack a folder and start a test run; returns its id, queue place, package SHA-256 and label (the git commit by default) | 150 |
| `cancel_run` | Cancel one of your runs that hasn't finished; only with `confirm: true` | 60 |
| `submit` | Pack a folder and submit it for a scored run, public and final; only with `confirm: true` after the person said yes | 100 |

Everything only reads, except `test_run`, `cancel_run` and `submit`, and `run_package` with `out`, which saves a file on your computer. A scored submission is public and can't be undone, and a cancelled run
doesn't come back, so `submit` and `cancel_run` refuse unless the call says `confirm: true`: tell your agent to ask
you first. Your agent sees only what your team sees on the run page; another team's run is "404: run not found".

Run tools take a run id (`run_...`), a test run id (`reh_...`) or a submission id (`sub_...`, meaning its latest run).
`run_package` takes the same ids; a submission id there means the package it submitted, which its runs ran.

## What it shows

`get_run` while a run waits, then once it failed:

```
run_8af0981b3710558a · test run on the public dataset · package 3f2a1c9e0b12 (2 files) "a41c2d9-dirty"
Status queued, phase queued
Queued: 2 runs ahead of yours, starts in about 3 min
...
Status failed, phase done · Failure: Run exited with code 0 without submitting an answer (no answer)
```

`run_llm_calls`:

```
run_0d7f1203b576189a · 86 model calls in a run of 16:22 · $0.4130
Time in calls 6:41 · latency p50 2.1s, p95 31s · at most 4 at once (at 02:13)
  anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5: 33 calls, $0.4126, 57,619 in (72,128 cached) / 5,867 out, 2:05 in calls
  openai/gpt-5-mini: 1 call, $0.0004, 1,845 in / 12 out, 1.2s in calls
Failures: openai: 52 failed (429 rate limited)

[02:10.4 +3.2s] anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 200 in 4,210 (cached 3,900) out 312 $0.00471 id=c_812
[02:13.9 +0.4s] openai 429 rate limited $0.00 id=c_815
```

`run_profile` (the screen columns are seconds the browser's screen was changing; `–` is still):

```
time   b1 in · screen  b2 in · screen  b3 in · screen  b4 in · screen  calls  in calls  busy  cost
02:00  6 · 21s         3 · 8.0s        10 · 44s        0 · –           14     1:02      48s   $0.0612
03:00  4 · 12s         0 · –           0 · –           2 · 3.5s        3      41s       38s   $0.0140
Critical path:
Longest stretches over 10 s with no input, no screen change and no model call in flight:
  03:12.4–04:40.1 (01:27)
    last line before: [03:11.9] stdout: mail TAN: waiting for the TAN message
Browsers that went quiet:
  browser 3: last screen change at 02:45.4, then nothing for 04:53 until the end
```

`diagnose_run` names the failure's class and the next step: `cancelled`, `no answer` (your agent system ended
without entering one: fix it, a rerun alone won't help), `agent exit` (see stderr), `timeout` (make it faster),
`answer rejected` (fix the answer's shape) or `platform` (not your agent system: rerun it as it is). A reason that
starts with "Setup" is agent.json's setup: `run_logs` with stream `setup` shows why. Where the platform records a
run's failure class, that one is used.

## Times

Times are on the run's clock, as the run page shows them: `02:13`, `1:02:13`, `3m20s` or `133` seconds from the
run's start, or an ISO 8601 time; durations are written the same way. The same time in the run page's address,
`?t=02:13`, opens the replay there. Links point at the platform's own address, whichever name the CLI talks to.

A screenshot is cut from the recording with ffmpeg on the platform. If the platform can't do that right now, the
CLI cuts it with your own ffmpeg (`brew install ffmpeg`, or `sudo apt install ffmpeg`); without one it says so and
links the replay. A time outside a recording gets its nearest frame and says so ("browser 1's recording covers
-00:03.7–07:48.9").

## What it can't do

- **Past frames of a live run.** The recording is stored after the run ends and collection finishes; until then `run_screenshot` shows each
  browser's latest live frame, about a second behind the screen (its time says when), and
  filmstrips and screen activity wait for the end. The run page's live view shows it moving.
- **Logs as they arrive.** Tools answer once; `wait_for_run` waits up to 600 s if your client allows long tool calls
  (Codex stops a tool after 60 s unless you raise `tool_timeout_sec`). In a terminal, `atira logs <run> --follow`
  streams a run's logs until it ends.
- **Log streams** are `setup`, `stdout`, `stderr` and `input`: errors are in `stderr` and in `get_run`/`diagnose_run`,
  screen activity is in `run_profile`.
- **Typed secrets.** Inputs show typed text with keys, tokens and your run's secrets masked.

From a terminal, `atira cancel <run>` cancels a run and `atira status` lists your submissions and test runs.

## Try it

Ask your agent things like:

- "Why did my last test run fail? Diagnose it, then show me the screen at the moment it went idle."
- "Where did the time go in run_19932ad4ade523e4? Which model calls were slowest?"
- "Compare my last two test runs: what changed in the score and the cost?"
- "Start a test run of ./my-agent, wait until it's running, and show me every browser's screen at 01:00."
- "Which files did my latest submission's package have? Save it to ./downloaded and diff it against ./my-agent."

This guide is at `$API/docs/mcp.md`.

1	# How a run works
2	
3	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
4	
5	A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
6	logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
7	scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
8	logins.
9	
10	## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
11	
12	RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
13	
14	1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
15	   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
16	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
17	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
18	   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
19	   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
20	   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
21	   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
22	   provider takes your own key.
23	   Nothing done with these logins counts.
24	   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
25	2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
26	   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
27	   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
28	   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
29	
30	## Inside a run
31	
32	1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
33	   returns:
34	   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
35	   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
36	   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
37	     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
38	   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
39	   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
40	   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
41	     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
42	   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
43	2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
44	   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
45	   provider's with your own key (below).
46	3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
47	   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
48	   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
49	   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
50	     it again.
51	   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
52	     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
53	
54	Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
55	(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
56	front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
57	
58	## LLM calls
59	
60	Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
61	Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
62	own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
63	API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
64	
65	The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
66	
67	```
68	$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
69	```
70	
71	`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
72	
73	| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
74	| --- | --- | --- |
75	| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
76	| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
77	| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
78	| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
79	| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
80	| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
81	| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
82	| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
83	| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
84	| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
85	
86	The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
87	each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
88	(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
89	
90	### Your key
91	
92	Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
93	(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
94	unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
95	not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
96	
97	With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
98	`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
99	as `x-api-key`:
100	
101	```python
102	from openai import OpenAI
103	
104	client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
105	```
106	
107	A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
108	the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
109	
110	```python
111	import os
112	from google import genai
113	
114	client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],

126	organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
127	key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
128	start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

130	**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
131	`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
132	(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
133	for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
134	`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
135	`401`.

138	context.

140	### How cost is measured
141	
142	Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
143	provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
144	An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
145	`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
146	that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
147	a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
148	providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
149	chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
150	an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
151	early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
152	endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
153	fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

159	
160	Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
161	`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
162	
163	```sh
164	curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \

168	```
169	
170	Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
171	Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
172	cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
173	`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
174	
175	## Scored run
176	
177	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
178	ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
179	[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
180	a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
181	`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
182	
183	- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
184	- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
185	- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
186	  and the websites.
187	- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
188	
189	1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
190	2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
191	   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
192	   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
193	   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
194	   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
195	   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
196	   right after setup:
197	
198	   ```json

200	   ```
201	
202	   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
203	   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
204	   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
205	
206	   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
207	   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
208	   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
209	   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
210	   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
211	   run that answered keeps its result.
212	3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.
213	
214	| Variable | Value |
215	| --- | --- |
216	| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
217	| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
218	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
219	| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
220	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
221	| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
222	| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
223	| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
224	| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
225	| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
226	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
227	| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
228	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
229	| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
230	| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
231	| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |

234	organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |

| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |

| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |

The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
ends without an answer scores 0.

## Browsers

The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:

```json
{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
```

`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |

**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
recording of each afterwards.

On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
browsers.

`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and

test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens

## Test it in the sandbox first

`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against

browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,

your team. Up to 4 test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
test-run slot at once.

## Linking your GitHub repository

code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.

settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
settings.

## Watching your submission

Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its

masked as `[private]`.

next upload is refused with `429`. Your **best complete** submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
**latest** one that passed review goes into the final run. Your other submissions stay in your history at
`$API/team`. Cancelling a submission's scored run ends that submission: it never completes, the leaderboard ignores it, and you

   still pass or disqualify a submission later; a disqualified one reads "disqualified", leaves the leaderboard and
   the final run, and your team page gives the organizers' reason.

   then your run command (timed).
3. **Ranking:** once the run has finished and review is passed, your submission appears on the leaderboard with its quality, cost and
   time; ineligible answers rank after every eligible one.

   (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected and disqualified ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same.    `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`.

page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:

1	# Answers and scoring
2	
3	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
4	
5	Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
6	ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
7	websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
8	isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
9	on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
10	
11	## Per run
12	
13	- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
14	- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
15	  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
16	- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
17	- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
18	
19	A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
20	is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
21	
22	## Leaderboard
23	
24	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
25	keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
26	complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
27	the run's own value.
28	
29	1. Eligible before ineligible.
30	2. Higher quality.
31	3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
32	   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
33	   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
34	4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
35	
36	On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
37	the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
38	
39	Test runs and scored runs on the public scenario `public-1` show your team the points for each part of the answer,
40	never the expected values. Runs on the private dataset show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
41	
42	## Final run
43	
44	When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
45	answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
46	
47	## Winners
48	
49	We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
50	
51	1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
52	2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
53	3. The elegance of the system.
54	
55	It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
56	latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
57	publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
58	public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
59	`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
60	
61	## RFQ scoring
62	
63	The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
64	`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
65	ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
66	project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
67	The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
68	omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
69	
70	| Part (a bid) | Points |
71	| --- | --- |
72	| Decision | 5 |
73	| Tender reference | 5 |
74	| Discount percent | 5 |
75	| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
76	| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
77	| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
78	| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
79	| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
80	
81	
82	For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
83	points but leaves the other fields their credit.
84	
85	Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
86	one position's share each.
87	
88	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
89	
90	The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
91	Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
92	`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
93	When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
94	Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
95	counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
96	It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
97	Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
98	Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
99	on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
100	
101	Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
102	the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
103	rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.
104

Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.

## Winners

We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:

1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
3. The elegance of the system.

It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).

## RFQ scoring

The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.

| Part (a bid) | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | 5 |
| Tender reference | 5 |
| Discount percent | 5 |
| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |


For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
points but leaves the other fields their credit.

Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
one position's share each.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.

Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

# Fair play

**Rules at a glance**

You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.

**Not allowed**

- **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
- **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
- **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
- **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.

**How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.

The details follow.

## Allowed

- Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
  amount of tokens.
  The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
  prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
  for SDK configuration.
- Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
- Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
- Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
- Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
  contexts inside them as you like.

## Not allowed

- Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
  rules you may use.
- A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
  page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
  and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
- Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
- Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
- Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
  to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
  On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
- Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.

## How it is checked

- **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
  isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
  result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
  marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
  and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
  The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
  the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
  a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
- **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
  (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
  "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
  organizers' reason.
- **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
- **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
  supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
  with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
  across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
  winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
- **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
  Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
- **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
- **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
  run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
- **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.

Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
get the team disqualified.

## Flagged results

A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
lists flagged results, without a rank.

91:## Public and private data
98:## Bid rules
102:1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
103:2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
104:3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
105:4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
106:5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
107:6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
108:7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
109:8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
110:9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
111:10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
112:11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
113:12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
114:13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
115:14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
116:15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
117:16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
118:17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
119:18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
120:19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
121:20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
122:21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
123:22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
124:23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
125:24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
126:25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
127:26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
128:27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
129:28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
130:29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.
132:## How a run works
136:1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
137:2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
138:3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
139:4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
140:5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.

98:## Bid rules
102:1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
103:2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
104:3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
105:4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
106:5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
107:6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
108:7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
109:8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
110:9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
111:10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
112:11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
113:12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
114:13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
115:14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
116:15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
117:16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
118:17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
119:18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
120:19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
121:20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
122:21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
123:22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
124:23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
125:24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
126:25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
127:26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
128:27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
129:28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
130:29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

# From RFQ to bid

**Turn a public tender into a correct, signed bid without a person touching it.**

You work for a German hydraulics manufacturer that wants to bid on a public tender for hydraulic cylinders. What you need is spread over four websites: the tender portal, a supplier portal with the buyer's specification, your company's ERP and the sales inbox. They behave like real business software, with logins, popups, session timeouts and outdated documents. Your agent reads all of it, applies the bid rules and enters one priced, signed bid in the tender portal.

**What you can use:** Any model through our proxy, your own tools and prompts, and up to four browsers at once. A model does the work in the sandbox: it finds its way through the websites and makes the decisions during the run. No fixed scripts, no crawlers, no copied values, no person helping.

**How you win:** Your bid has to be eligible first. After that, the most accurate bid wins, and between equally accurate bids, the cheaper and faster one. The leaderboard uses the public data. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Challenge id | `rfq` |
| Version | `6` |
| Websites | 4 |
| Test run time limit | 2 hours |
| Scored run time limit | 20 minutes |
| Runs per submission | 1 |
| Public scenario | `public-1` |
| Answer | entered on the `tender-portal` website |
| Largest answer | 65,536 bytes |

## Quick start for agents

Set the platform URL, install the CLI and sign in once: `atira login` opens the browser, where you approve a personal token for this device (`atira login --device` prints a link and a code instead, for a machine without a browser; plain curl uses the [device flow](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in)). Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

# or without installing: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
atira login   # approve in the browser

eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites, to run your agent locally
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq   # one sandbox run on the public dataset, opened live

- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your company's materials, stock, lead times and price conditions with validity periods and quantity scales.
- What makes it hard: SAP-style transaction codes, an F4 search popup, status codes, a short session timeout.

### 4. Webmail (Werkpost, `mail`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-mail.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your sales inbox, with the sales director's discount approval and the signing TAN.
- What makes it hard: Look-alike approvals for other tenders, superseded approvals, an archive folder, paging.

132	## How a run works
133	
134	Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).
135	
136	1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
137	2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
138	3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
139	4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
140	5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.
141	
142	### Develop locally
143	
144	```sh
145	eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites
146	curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting"   # the same, with the brief, as JSON
147	# run your agent on your machine, then once in the sandbox:
148	atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq
149	```
150	
151	`atira scout --env` exports the scouting logins as `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the shape a run gets), each website's URL, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the brief and the answer format. It also points the free hosted models at `atira models proxy` on your computer, so your agent needs no model key; another provider takes your own. Nothing done there counts. With these logins, an answer entered on the tender portal is acknowledged but never counts. In a run, your agent reads the same at `GET /v1/runs/current` with the run token as `x-api-key`, and hands in one valid answer of up to 65,536 bytes; a malformed one returns its problems while the clock keeps running.
152	
153	### Read the run
154	
155	Inside a test or scored run, with the run token (`$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`) in `RUN_TOKEN`:
156	
157	```sh
158	curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/current" -H "x-api-key: $RUN_TOKEN"
159	```
160	
161	The response holds `brief` (the task in Markdown, with the rules), `access` (each website's `url` and `credentials`), `submission` (where the answer goes), `answer_schema`, `expires_at`, `llm_proxy_url` and `llm_providers`. Outside a run, `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` returns the brief, logins, answer target and schema for the public websites, without a token.
162	
163	### In the sandbox
164	
165	A test run and a scored run start your `run` command with these variables. `setup` runs before, with network but without them, for up to 5 minutes that don't count toward your time.
166	
167	| Variable | Value |
168	| --- | --- |
169	| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the platform API; the run is at /v1/runs/current |
